config.title: Implement Stack using Queues

intro.title: Implement Stack using Queues
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a stack data structure using only two queues. You'll learn how to simulate the Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) behavior of a stack by manipulating elements with queue operations like enqueue and dequeue. The main technologies involved are JavaScript arrays (to represent queues) and functions for push and pop operations. This exercise will help you understand how different data structures can be implemented using others, enhancing your problem-solving skills in algorithms.
intro.usecase: While implementing a stack using queues might seem abstract, this pattern appears in real-world systems where you need to simulate LIFO behavior using existing FIFO infrastructure. For example, in message queue systems like RabbitMQ or Kafka, developers sometimes need to process the most recent messages first while working within queue-based architectures. This technique is also useful in UI frameworks where you need to manage undo/redo functionality or navigation history using queue-based state management tools. Understanding this implementation helps developers work within architectural constraints while maintaining required data processing behaviors.

objectives: Implement a stack class using two queue data structures
Configure the push operation to maintain stack behavior with queue operations
Manipulate queue elements to simulate stack pop functionality
Initialize stack properties and maintain internal queue states
Construct the peek operation using only queue methods
Apply queue operations to check if the stack is empty
Integrate all stack methods into a cohesive class structure

content.body: Have you ever wondered how to build one data structure using another? Today we'll implement a Stack using only Queues. This clever exercise helps you understand both structures deeply.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
1. Explain the LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) behavior of a stack.
2. Explain the FIFO (First-In, First-Out) behavior of a queue.
3. Implement a stack's push and pop operations using only queue operations.
4. Compare the efficiency of different approaches.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you're stacking plates. You add a clean plate to the top of the pile. When you need a plate, you take it from the top. This is a stack: the last plate you put on is the first one you take off (LIFO).
content.title: Think about it

content.body: Now picture people waiting in line at a coffee shop. The first person to join the line is the first one served. This is a queue: first in, first out (FIFO).
content.title: Now imagine a line

content.body: Your challenge: Can you simulate the plate-stacking behavior (LIFO) using only the coffee-line behavior (FIFO)? How would you make a 'last in, first out' system with 'first in, first out' components?
content.title: The challenge

content.body: You just thought about how two different ordering principles work. A stack reverses order (last becomes first), while a queue preserves order (first stays first).
content.title: What you considered

content.body: In programming, we often need to choose the right tool. Stacks are great for undo operations or parsing expressions. Queues handle tasks fairly. Understanding how to build one from the other reveals their core differences.
content.title: Why it matters

content.body: The trick is to use queues to reverse the order. Since queues give us the oldest element first, we can move elements between queues to make the newest element accessible. Think of it like rearranging the coffee line so the newest person gets served first.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Stack: pile of plates. Queue: people in a line.

content.body: We'll maintain two queues. When we push a new element, we'll add it to an empty queue, then transfer all elements from the other queue to this one. This keeps the newest element at the front of the queue, simulating stack behavior.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize two empty queues.
2. For push(x): Add x to empty queue, then move all elements from the other queue to this one.
3. For pop(): Remove and return the front element from the non-empty queue.
4. For top(): Return the front element without removing it.
5. For empty(): Check if both queues are empty.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the Stack class
steps.instruction: Start by creating a class called MyStack. Inside the constructor, initialize two empty arrays to act as our queues. Name them queue1 and queue2.
steps.hint: Remember, arrays in JavaScript can work as queues using push (to add to back) and shift (to remove from front).
steps.expectedOutcome: A class with two empty array properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the basic structure with two queues.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure both queue1 and queue2 are initialized as empty arrays.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start simple: create two empty array properties in the constructor.

steps.title: Implement push method
steps.instruction: Add a push(x) method. The strategy: add x to the empty queue, then move all elements from the other queue to this one. This keeps x at the front.
steps.hint: First check which queue is empty, add x to it, then use a while loop to transfer elements from the other queue.
steps.expectedOutcome: Method that correctly maintains stack order using two queues.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! You've implemented the clever queue transfer to maintain LIFO order.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you're moving ALL elements from the non-empty queue to the queue with the new element.
steps.feedbackWrong: Think about it: add the new element to an empty queue, then bring over all existing elements.

steps.title: Implement pop method
steps.instruction: Add a pop() method. Since push ensures the newest element is at the front of the active queue, we just need to remove and return the front element from the non-empty queue.
steps.hint: Check which queue has elements and use shift() to remove and return the first element.
steps.expectedOutcome: Method that removes and returns the top element (last pushed).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You're correctly accessing the front of the active queue, which holds the most recent element.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're checking which queue has elements and returning the shifted value.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: the newest element is at the front of whichever queue has elements. Use shift() to get it.

steps.title: Implement top method
steps.instruction: Add a top() method. This should return the top element (most recently pushed) without removing it. Similar to pop, but don't remove the element.
steps.hint: Check which queue has elements and return the first element without shifting it.
steps.expectedOutcome: Method that returns the top element without removal.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You're accessing the element correctly without modifying the queue.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good. Make sure you're returning the element, not removing it with shift().
steps.feedbackWrong: For top(), just peek at the first element of the non-empty queue. Use array indexing.

steps.title: Implement empty method
steps.instruction: Add an empty() method that returns true if the stack is empty, false otherwise. The stack is empty when both queues are empty.
steps.hint: Simply check if both queue1 and queue2 have length 0.
steps.expectedOutcome: Method that correctly checks if both queues are empty.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your stack implementation is now complete.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. The stack is empty only when BOTH queues are empty.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check both queue1 and queue2 lengths. If both are 0, return true.

content.body: Congratulations! You've implemented a stack using only queues. Remember: stacks are LIFO (like plates), queues are FIFO (like lines). By moving elements between queues, we reverse the order. Push is O(n) because we transfer all elements, while pop and top are O(1). This trade-off shows how different data structures have different strengths.
